# A Brief Refresher on the Mathematical Foundations of Navigation

This foundations section is a reference and refresher for material students are expected to already know coming into the class. Modern autonomous navigation systems rely heavily on estimation theory, which in turn relies on probability theory and linear algebra. If you are rusty on these topics, please review the relevant chapters in the Foundations part of the notes. A modern autonomous navigation system is often a piece of digital software running on a computer. Therefore, we also include a chapter on modern Python programming, which is the language we will be using for all of our code examples and assignments in this class. While there are practical considerations that make it such that Python is not the best choice language to use in production for an autonomous navigation system, it is a great language for learning and prototyping. The concepts we will be covering in this class are not specific to Python, and can be implemented in any programming language. Furthermore, the scientific Python ecosystem (`numpy`, `scipy`, `matplotlib`, etc.) provides a powerful set of tools for implementing and experimenting with the concepts we will be covering in this class. Many componets of that ecosystem are implemented in C under the hood, so we still get good performance while writing code in Python that enables us to focus on learning the concepts of autonomous inertial navigation and good software engineering practices, without having to get too bogged down in the details of memory management and other low-level programming concerns that come with using a high performance lower-level language like C, C++, or Rust.

If you wish to have a greater challenge when implementing the projects, you are encouraged to try using a lower-level language like C, C++, or Rust for the assignments. This will give you a deeper understanding of the performance considerations and trade-offs involved in real-world autonomous navigation systems. In practice, as of this writing in the summer of 2026, many real-world autonomous navigation systems are implemented in a combination of C and C++ for the performance benefits it provides, while still having a rich ecosystem of libraries and tools for software development. That said, there is a growing trend towards using Rust in performance-critical applications like autonomous navigation, due to its strong safety guarantees, modern language features and developer tooling, all while maintaining high performance and guaranteeing memory safety. If you wish to have a career in autonomous navigation, eventually you will need to be proficient in at least one of these lower-level languages. While I personally prefer Rust over C and C++ for new projects, there is a much larger ecosystem of libraries, tools, and legacy navigation code available in C and C++. I won't make any specific recommendations on which language to learn and in which order, but I would strongly suggest that you eventually get around to being proficient in C++ to get your foot in the door for many navigation jobs, and then learn Rust as well to be able to work on the cutting edge of navigation software development.
